subject: Random temporal effects in a year-stratified N-mixture model

messages.author: 074a030d0cd7e490
messages.subject: Random temporal effects in a year-stratified N-mixture model
parts:
Hello,

Colleague Paula Ledezma and I, are analyzing Quetzal counts made over eight years in a Central-American location. We fit a year-stratified N-mixture model with a temporal trend on lambda (as described in chapter 2 of AHM2) and found a slight suggestion of an upward trend. Because the evidence is not overwhelming, it occurred to us that it would be interesting to let lambda vary randomly over time to see if the suggestion of an upward trend resurfaced in the randomly varying lambdas. And yes, we are aware that we could estimate one independent lambda per year for a similar inquiry, but we believe that enough biology is shared among years to justify a random temporal effect.

To build this random temporal effect, we added a random error term to the log(lambda) equation, with mean = 0 and sigma based on a uniform prior bounded by 0 and 2 (as in chapter 4 of Kéry and Schaub’s 2012 ‘BPA using WinBUGS’ book). The results are not good, it looks like the model has trouble converging on a variance (actually tau) for the random error term.

Has anyone seen this problem? We are finding it strange that no one seems to be putting random temporal effects on year-stratified N-mixture models. Is it dumb to try? Why?

Thank you for any feedback!

Gonçalo

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: Random temporal effects in a year-stratified N-mixture model
parts:
Dear Goncalo,

from what I understand I don't think you're doing anything wrong. But it may be that with only 8 years, a variance may be hard to estimate for the latent abundance. Also, using what some call "weakly informative" priors can often help with convergence. So, for instance, if the data say that a random year variance in log lambda is 0.25, then putting a U(0,1) prior may still be quite vague, but help getting convergence a lot. Another, even more "suggestive" prior in that case might be some more triangular distribution, such as a half-Cauchy (= t with 1 d.f.) or half-normal.

Best regards --- Marc
